channel.title: Brain Blog – try4ever.com
channel.description: Notes on studying, memory and building Brain – a 3D knowledge map tool for students.

item.title: Data Science: The Math, Mapped
item.description: You can import everything – the understanding is still manual. Linear algebra, calculus and probability, self-taught at night, finally hold together on a map.

item.title: Police & Fire Exams: Mapped
item.description: The physical test is the easy part – the written exam decides who waits another year. Reading comprehension, math and judgment, all scenario-shaped.

item.title: Hard Books: Finish Them This Time
item.description: Every ambitious reader owns a graveyard: Sapiens abandoned at page 60, Thinking, Fast and Slow at page 90. The books weren't too hard. The map was missing.

item.title: Seminary: The Reading Mountain
item.description: Hebrew paradigms, Greek participles, systematic theology, church history – and a sermon due Sunday. Seminary is the densest reading list in graduate education.

item.title: Dyslexia: Maps Over Walls
item.description: Reading isn't the problem. Reading forty pages of dense prose and then being tested on it is. When the walls come down, the structure underneath is yours.

item.title: Private Pilot: The Written Test, Mapped
item.description: 60 questions, 70 percent to pass – and your instructor keeps saying it's all in the PHAK. It is. It's just also in the FAR/AIM, the charts and the weather manual.

item.title: Trades Exams: The Code Book, Mapped
item.description: Open-book exam sounds like mercy until you meet the National Electrical Code – hundreds of pages, reprinted every three years, and a clock running.

item.title: PMP: ITTOs Into a Map
item.description: 35 contact hours to enter, about 180 questions to exit, and an exam that loves agile as much as a Gantt chart. The ITTOs are unmanageable as lists and obvious as a map.

item.title: Series 7: The Options Mountain
item.description: The SIE was the warm-up. The Series 7 top-off is the mountain: suitability, options strategies and rules on rules. Chains, in other words. Maps win chains.

item.title: Real Estate: License Without Tears
item.description: Decades of prelicensing hours, a national portion, a state portion, and pass rates that hover near half. The exam tests vocabulary of ownership – vocabulary is structure.

item.title: State Tests: Regents & STAAR, Mapped
item.description: Spring arrives with the acronym – Regents, STAAR, MCAS, CAASPP – and a year of material to prove. Families get the map; students get the plan.

item.title: Gaokao: Three Years, One Map
item.description: More than thirteen million register each year, three years of high school compressed into two days of exams. 一轮 to 三轮 – run them on a map.

item.title: UPSC: The Whole Syllabus, Mapped
item.description: Prelims, mains, interview – and a syllabus with no natural boundary. Roughly a thousand final selections against applicants in the hundreds of thousands. Structure is the strategy.

item.title: Anatomy & Physiology: The Gauntlet
item.description: 206 bones, hundreds of muscles, and the pituitary keeps making cameo appearances everywhere. A&P is the prereq that decides who feels ready in nursing school.

item.title: Statistics: From Fog to Map
item.description: Statistics is the course people postpone to the last semester. Then the last semester arrives. A map turns test-choice panic into a decision tree you can see.

item.title: Organic Chemistry: Mechanisms, Mapped
item.description: If orgo were about memorizing reactions, everyone would pass. It's about seeing where the electrons go – and that's a picture, not a paragraph.

item.title: ASWB: Social Work Boards, Mapped
item.description: Four exam categories, decades of theories, an ethics code with legs. The ASWB exam rewards knowing which knowledge to bring into which vignette.

item.title: NBCOT: OT Boards, Mapped
item.description: The OTR exam doesn't ask what occupational therapy is. It asks what you'd do Tuesday morning with a stroke patient and a stubborn kitchen.

item.title: Vet Boards: NAVLE & VTNE, Mapped
item.description: Classes taught one species at a time. The NAVLE examines every species at once. Maps are how the cross-species connections finally show up.

item.title: Shelf Exams: Survive the Rotation
item.description: Six weeks of wards, then an NBME shelf on the whole specialty. The clerkship teaches the work; a map teaches the test behind the work.

item.title: ESL Students: Textbooks, Mapped
item.description: First you learn the language. Then they ask you to learn medicine, law or IT in it. By most estimates over a billion people are studying English right now – see the ideas first, translate less.

item.title: Actuarial Exams: 300 Hours, Mapped
item.description: The classic rule: 100 study hours per exam hour, pass rates near half. Over a multi-year exam chain, structure isn't optional – it's the syllabus.

item.title: Tutors: More Students, Same Hours
item.description: Five students, five subjects, five prep sessions – every Sunday. Private tutoring runs on one bottleneck: you. Structure your material and scale without burning out.

item.title: Corporate Training: Knowledge That Sticks
item.description: Your onboarding deck was beautiful. Ask a new hire what it said a week later. The forgetting curve doesn't care about your slides – map the knowledge instead.

item.title: Homeschool: One Map per Year
item.description: Roughly one in twenty American students learns at home. Give each year a visible map, so you can prove – and celebrate – what was actually covered.

item.title: ADHD: Maps Beat Willpower
item.description: When starting is the hard part and walls of text slide right off, a spatial map gives your attention a door. Visible structure, visible progress, no shame.

item.title: Changing Careers? Study Like a Pro
item.description: Retraining at 30, 40 or 50 means becoming a student again – usually with a mortgage and a calendar. You have more study skill than you think. Point it at a map.

item.title: PhD Students: Map the Literature
item.description: Millions of papers publish every year and your committee wants synthesis, not summaries. Map the field's arguments instead of stacking PDFs.

item.title: Finals Week: From Cramming to Calm
item.description: All-nighters feel heroic and perform terribly. Finals week, rebuilt in four evenings: map it, quiz it, space it, sleep.

item.title: Developers: Docs Into a Map
item.description: New stack on Monday, docs longer than the codebase. Feed the PDFs and EPUBs into a 3D map and see the architecture before the syntax.

item.title: IT Certs: Security+ to AWS, Mapped
item.description: Ports, protocols, acronyms in ALL CAPS. Certification exams sound like soup because you're studying soup – domains and how they connect is the fix.

item.title: GRE & GMAT: Admissions Without Fog
item.description: Years out of school, studying after work, rusty quant and decayed vocabulary. The GRE and GMAT reward structure over stamina – here's the structure.

item.title: IB Diploma: Six Subjects, No Fog
item.description: Six subjects, TOK, the Extended Essay, CAS – the IB is coordination overload. Maps keep every thread visible at once.

item.title: JEE & NEET: Two Years, One Map
item.description: Roughly two and a half million register for NEET-UG and over a million for JEE Main. The syllabus is two years deep. Structure is survival.

item.title: ASVAB: Map Your Way to the Job
item.description: Your ASVAB line scores decide which military jobs you can train for. Map the subtests that feed the score you actually need.

item.title: Parents: See Your Child's Real Progress
item.description: 'I already studied, mom.' Meta-analyses link family involvement to real achievement gains – if you can see the studying. Now you can.

item.title: NREMT: Scenarios That Finally Click
item.description: The NREMT asks about evolving patients, not isolated facts. If you studied protocols as lists, the scenarios felt like ambushes. Un-ambush them.

item.title: INBDE: Dental Boards, Mapped
item.description: The INBDE replaced the two-part NBDE with one integrated exam. Integration is exactly what a map does – so study integrated.

item.title: NAPLEX: Hundreds of Drugs, One Map
item.description: Pharmacology is taught as lists and tested as judgment. A map turns hundreds of drugs from alphabet soup into landscape.

item.title: NPTE: Map the Whole Body
item.description: You learned the body in pieces – ortho here, neuro there, cardio somewhere else. The NPTE hands you whole patients. Maps reassemble them.

item.title: Teachers: Cut the Busywork, Keep the Craft
item.description: Teachers work about 53 hours a week. AI should sharpen your craft, never replace it – here's a tool that takes the busywork, not the teaching.

item.title: PANCE: Ten Systems, One Map
item.description: The PANCE blueprint spreads hundreds of conditions across ten organ systems – but rotations taught them to you one ward at a time. Reconnect them.

item.title: Nursing School: Care Plans Without Panic
item.description: Clinicals by day, care plans by night, pharmacology somewhere in between. Nursing school is a systems problem – give it a map.

item.title: FE Exam: Engineering Formulas, Mapped
item.description: The FE exam spans a dozen disciplines in one day. Thermodynamics, statics, ethics, econ – mapped, they finally behave like one subject.

item.title: Language Exams: Map Your Way to Fluency
item.description: IELTS, TOEFL, JLPT, DELE – language exams test grammar in motion. Grammar patterns, vocab families and keigo all map beautifully.

item.title: GCSE & A-Levels: Revision You Can See
item.description: Revision guides pile up, exam boards differ, and 'just revise' helps nobody. GCSE and A-Level students: make the revision visible.

item.title: AP, SAT, ACT: Big Exams, Small Panic
item.description: AP exams, the SAT and the ACT reward students who can see structure. High schoolers: here's how to study smarter, not just longer.

item.title: CPA & CFA: Mountains of Material, Mapped
item.description: Accounting and finance exams bury you in standards and formulas. Maps turn FAR, AUD, REG and the CFA curriculum into visible structure.

item.title: Law Exams: See the Whole Case Map
item.description: Law school hides its structure inside hundreds of pages. IRAC, elements and exceptions become navigable when you can see the case map.

item.title: NCLEX Pharmacology That Finally Sticks
item.description: 317,710 candidates sat the NCLEX last year – and a 73% pass rate means most walk in under-prepared. Pharmacology is where maps win.

item.title: MCAT Prep: Stop Rereading, Start Retrieving
item.description: More than 23,000 students matriculate into U.S. med schools each year – most of them beat the MCAT with retrieval, not rereading.

item.title: USMLE Step 1 Without the All-Nighter
item.description: About 25,000 U.S. and Canadian students take Step 1 every year. The exam tests connections, not lists – study it that way.

item.title: Spaced Repetition vs 3D Maps: Use Both
item.description: Flashcard schedules and 3D maps solve different problems. The strongest study systems refuse to choose – here's how to combine them.

item.title: Watch Your Mastery Turn From Red to Green
item.description: A progress bar you can see in 3D changes which topics you study next – and it changes how it feels to walk into an exam.

item.title: Why I Built Brain: Notes Into 3D Maps
item.description: Outlines hide the shape of what you're learning. I wanted to see it – so I built a tool that turns your own files into a 3D map.

item.title: The Chat That Changed How I Study
item.description: Two friends. One drowning in notes, one calm before finals. One question in a coffee shop that reveals the entire difference.

item.title: 5 Study Hacks That Actually Survived Testing
item.description: Forget highlighters. Five unconventional study hacks that survived contact with real evidence – including one that involves walking in circles.

item.title: What a Learning Coach Told Me About Systems
item.description: A seasoned learning coach on why motivation is overrated, why systems win, and the three questions to ask before any study session.

item.title: Reading Five Times Is the Worst Way to Study
item.description: Rereading feels productive and delivers almost nothing. The 61%-vs-40% study every student should know – and the 20-minute fix.

item.title: Drowning in Lecture Notes? Here's the Fix
item.description: I used to hate studying. Then I learned to see my whole syllabus at once – and the stack of PDFs turned into a map I could walk.

item.title: Rote Memorization Fails. Your Brain Wants This
item.description: Repeating facts until they hurt is the hardest way to learn. What research says works instead – and how to switch tonight.

item.title: A Poem for Every Tired Student
item.description: Your hippocampus is a constellation of memories. A short poem for the nights when studying feels like falling – and a way back up.

item.title: Why a Map Beats a List for Memory
item.description: Your brain is a navigator, not a filing cabinet. Spatial memory turns lists you forget into places you know – here's the science and the shortcut.
